notes.meaning: David wrote this while hiding in the desert of Judah, either running from King Saul or later from his son Absalom. He begins by calling God "my God," claiming God as his very own through God's promise to him. The word for "earnestly" is linked to the word for dawn, so it means both eager and early in the morning. His soul and body together, his whole self, long for God the way a thirsty man longs for water in a dry land far from God's house of worship.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars doubt the title. They think the desert is a word picture, and the psalm was written by someone in exile longing for the temple, perhaps near the time Jerusalem fell.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine's Latin Bible read "desert of Idumea." He took this desert to mean this world and the hard life we live in it now.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: In Orthodox churches this is counted as Psalm 62. It is one of six psalms read at the start of the morning prayer service. The early church also sang it as its morning psalm.

notes.meaning: David remembers times in God's house of worship when he saw God's power and glory. What he missed most was not the ceremonies but God himself. Now, out in the desert, he looks for that same closeness with God. He trusts that God can be met by faith anywhere, even far from the sanctuary.

"Loving devotion" means God's loyal, faithful love that keeps his promises. David says this love is worth more than life itself, more than health, wealth, or a long life. Since God's love is that precious, David's lips will praise him even in hard times.

differ.view: The contrast is between the comfortable life people lean on and God's mercy, which holds up those about to sink. We should trust that mercy even when facing death, more than anything that looks like life.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine noted the Hebrew says "lives" and took it to mean the many ways of life people choose, like business or farming. God's one life, given by his mercy and not earned, is better than all of them.

notes.meaning: David promises to praise God for the rest of his life, not just for a moment. Lifting the hands was the usual way of praying and worshipping in Israel. Doing it "in Your name" means praying and praising with an eye on who God has shown himself to be, and leaning on his strength.

differ.view: Raising hands in worship has clear Bible support here and elsewhere. It shows that we depend completely on God.
Raising hands is fine, but churches should not make people feel they must do it to seem spiritual. What matters most is that the hands are holy.
Some use this verse to push back against stiff, formal worship and to urge believers to raise their hands.
